title: Can It Drive There: Slope and Roughness From a Height Map, Judged Against What This Vehicle's Motors, Tyres and Wheels Can Do

questions.question: Which two properties of the ground does a height map give?
questions.explanation: A plane through the 3 by 3 cells gives the slope, and the spread of the heights about it the roughness. A ramp has one and a field of stones the other.

questions.question: A ramp of 10 degrees was read as:
questions.explanation: The plane fit recovered the ramp's slope with no roughness, and the same when the ramp ran along the other axis.

questions.question: The reference vehicle's slope limit on gravel was:
options: 25.6 degrees, what the motors can climb
22.3 degrees, the smaller of the motors, the grip and the balance
questions.explanation: The motors could start on 25.6 degrees and gravel holds 22.3. The limit is the least of motors, grip and balance.

questions.question: A slope of 24 degrees on gravel had a cost of:
questions.explanation: On tarmac the same ramp cost 198 and could be driven. Gravel holds only 22.3 degrees, so 24 is past the limit and lethal.

questions.question: Why does the cost rise with the square of the share of the limit?
options: To match the costs of the inflation layer
Because slope is measured in degrees
It is nearly free for most of the range and steep near the limit
So that roughness counts for more than slope
questions.explanation: Half the limit costs a quarter of the scale, so ordinary ground is cheap and the cost climbs sharply only near what the vehicle cannot do.

questions.question: Why can a tall vehicle be limited by its balance and not its grip?
options: It tips at atan(half the track over the height of its centre of mass), which falls as it gets taller
questions.explanation: The tipping slope is the arctangent of half the track over the height of the centre of mass. Raise the centre and that angle can fall below the grip's.
